summary: TERRA-TWIN DEVON is an open-source Python tool that helps find and characterize terrestrial analogs for future Moon and Mars landing sites and bases. It uses NASA elevation data from LOLA (Moon) and MOLA (Mars), together with ArcticDEM for Devon Island’s Haughton Crater. It puts each terrain on a common grid and computes slope, elevation variability, local relief and roughness. It then compares the terrains with transparent metrics: distribution overlap, Wasserstein distance and the KS statistic. A second tool, the Terrestrial Analog Finder, ranks Earth locations against a lunar or Martian target, scoring terrain, thermal and aridity factors separately using NASA MODIS temperature and vegetation data. Mission teams rely on a small number of analog sites that are not fully characterized. Our tool gives them a reproducible, data-driven way to describe and rank more candidates before costly field tests. All code is public on GitHub: https://github.com/Sbarrientos-creator/TERRA-TWIN-DEVON
details:
The project has two Streamlit apps and an offline data pipeline.

  • The Devon Analyzer takes GeoTIFF elevation files for Haughton Crater and a Moon or Mars crater. It reprojects each file into a local equal-area, meter-based map using the correct planetary radius, resamples them to the same resolution and window size, and removes regional tilt so that different elevation datums do not distort the comparison. It then calculates slope, detrended elevation variability, local relief and roughness, and compares the two terrains with overlap, Wasserstein distance and the KS statistic, with histograms and a data-provenance table.
  • The Terrestrial Analog Finder uses a table of Earth locations built from NASA MODIS and other open data. It scores each location against a Moon or Mars target on three separate factor groups (terrain, thermal, aridity/biology), with user-adjustable weights, and shows the best matches on a world map with a radar chart for each.
  • The offline pipeline downloads and processes the data so that the apps only read small result files, which keeps them fast and reproducible.Benefits and intended impact
    Analog sites are used to test equipment and methods before flights, but many are not well characterized. The tool gives mission planners a transparent way to see which aspects of a site (terrain, temperature, dryness) resemble a lunar or Martian target and which do not, instead of one unexplained similarity number. We want it to help teams shortlist and justify analog sites for rover and habitat testing.

Tools and technologies
Python, Streamlit, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Plotly, pyproj, Google Earth Engine, NASA Earthdata (earthaccess), QGIS/GDAL for checking files, pytest for testing, and GitHub for collaboration.

What is creative about it

  • Each factor group is scored separately, because no Earth site matches the Moon or Mars on everything.
  • The comparison uses slope, relief and roughness rather than raw elevation, which solves the problem of different vertical reference surfaces on three worlds.
  • Known analogs (Haughton, Atacama, Death Valley, the Dry Valleys) are used as a validation check on the ranking.

Factors we considered
Different map projections, resolutions and elevation datums on each body; the same window size and scale for every comparison; the 463 m native resolution of the MOLA data; the fact that MODIS and precipitation data do not cover polar regions equally; and the fact that Earth has an atmosphere, different gravity and different radiation. Slopes were tested against known synthetic terrain, and results are reproducible with a fixed random seed.

Status and limitations
This is a working prototype. The terrain statistics and ranking code are tested on synthetic terrain. Comparisons are of terrain morphology only, and we do not claim overall planetary similarity. Further work includes the four Devon research zones (impact structure, rim, canyons and valleys, polar desert), Diviner and THEMIS temperature data, and lava-tube and resource layers.
